extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / experimental scientists (readers of Philosophical Transactions) interested in optics, light, and colour theory
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating theories of light and colour
extracted.subtask_description: Formulating, testing, and critiquing hypotheses about light, refraction, and colours using prism experiments, quantitative comparison of optical errors, and careful experimental controls. Emphasises experimental demonstration over speculative hypothesis and gives methods to distinguish primary (original) from compound colours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat hypotheses modestly; avoid asserting unproven mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make a fundamental supposition about the mechanism of light (e.g., its corporeity) unless explained and supported; treat such ideas as plausible consequences at most, not as fundamental assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘I do it without any absolute positiveness, as the word perhaps intimates; and make it at most but a very plausible consequence of the doctrine, and not a fundamental supposition… I chose to decline them all, and to speak of light in general terms, considering it abstractly… without determining what that thing is.’ — prefer speaking of light abstractly and avoid committing to untested mechanical hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use countervailing/reflexive experiments to rule out apparatus irregularities
rubrics_metrics.description: Design experiments that cancel or reverse prior effects to reveal whether observed phenomena are regular consequences or contingent irregularities of the apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ‘to prevent the suspicion of any such irregularities, I refracted the light contrarywise with two prisms successively, to destroy thereby the regular effects of the first prism by the second, and to discover the irregular effects by augmenting them with iterated refractions.’ If splitting/diluting occurred, the second prism would further dilate the image; because it did not, one concludes the refractions follow a constant law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-orientation prism test to detect splitting/dilution of rays
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the second prism transverse (rotated) to the first to see whether cross refractions produce an expected geometric dilation if rays had been split into superficial or pyramidal forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘I sometimes placed the second prism in a position transverse to the first, on design to try, if it would make the long image become four-square… If… the refraction of the first prism did, by splitting, dilate a linear ray into a superficial, the cross refractions of that second prism ought… to draw that superficial ray into a pyramidal solid. But, upon trial, I found otherwise; the image being as regularly oblong as before.’ Use geometric predictions vs observation to falsify splitting hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce theoretical disputes to specific testable queries
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame the central theoretical disagreements as a small number of clear, experimentally addressable questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton reduces the debate to three queries: (1) Whether unequal refractions are due to different refrangibility of rays or to splitting/rarefying of the same ray; (2) Whether there are more than two sorts of colours; (3) Whether whiteness is a mixture of all colours. This focuses experimental design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish primary (original) vs compound colours by refrangibility and stability
rubrics_metrics.description: A primary (original) colour cannot be changed by any art and its rays are alike refrangible; a compound colour is changeable and its rays are not alike refrangible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test: view the colour through a prism — if edges are tinged with other colours or the colour is transformed when refracted, it is compound; if it remains distinct and uniformly the same to the edges, it is original. ‘That colour is primary or original, which cannot by any art be changed, and whose rays are alike refrangible…’

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret coloured transmission experiments accounting for thickness and selective transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: When colours arise from transmitted light through liquids or films, account for thickness-dependent selective transmission rather than assuming a small set of only original colours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of Hooke's wedge-box experiment: tincture of aloes and solutions show different colours at different thicknesses (yellow near edges, red where thicker); thus apparent variety arises from selective interception/transmission of rays, not necessarily from only two original colours. ‘The tincture of aloes… appeared yellow near the edge of the box, and red at other places where it was thicker…’

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer ontological parsimony (only two original colours) from capacity to compound
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if many colours can be produced by mixing two given coloured media, that does not prove those two are the only original colours or the sole origin of all colours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two reasons given: (1) the two used liquids are themselves compound of other colours; (2) even if they were original, other routes may produce the same colours. Avoid begging the question by assuming components are primitive simply because they combine to produce others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirically quantify and compare optical aberrations when choosing designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare quantitative errors (e.g., focus errors across apertures) for alternative optical constructions (reflecting vs refracting) and prefer the construction with demonstrably smaller errors for intended apertures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton computes a table comparing errors of reflecting concave and refracting convex surfaces across aperture sizes and concludes refracting convex errors are far greater in large apertures; thus prefers reflection in theory for certain constructions. Use measured/calculated tables to guide instrument design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require experiment and demonstration to support fluid/aether mechanical hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept mechanical ether/wave hypotheses that claim straight-line propagation of vibrations without showing experimental or demonstrative support; such claims may be impossible (waves tend to spread).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘The fundamental supposition itself seems impossible; namely, that the waves or vibrations of any fluid can… be propagated in straight lines, without a continual and very extravagant spreading… I mistake if there be not both experiment and demonstration to the contrary.’ Theoretical plausibility must be backed by experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use intercepting and selective interception tests to analyze ray composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Intercept portions of refracted images or beams individually (e.g., by intercepting rays severally) to test whether parts behave as independent rays or as fragments of a previously single ray.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘…those linear diverging parts depend not on one another for the manner of their refraction, but are every one of them as truly and completely rays as the whole was, before its incidence; as may appear by intercepting them severally.’ Practical method for validating whether aggregated rays are genuine independent rays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer explanations that explain the phenomena without unnecessary multiplicity of entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply methodological economy: avoid multiplying entities (postulating additional kinds of things) unless necessary to explain phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘And if those original inequalities may suffice to differ the rays in colour and refrangibility, I see no reason why they that adhere to any of those hypotheses, should seek for other causes of these effects, unless… they will multiply entities without necessity.’ Use parsimony as a guide in theory choice.
